A golden handshake is a large, generous financial payment given to a senior executive or employee when they leave a company — whether they are fired, forced to retire, or choose to leave as part of a deal.

Think of it as the company's way of saying: "Here is a big goodbye gift for your years of service and loyalty."
Breaking Down the Name

The word "golden" means valuable, generous, and financially rich. In the business world, anything "golden" refers to a high-value financial deal or benefit given to top-level people.

The word "handshake" traditionally symbolizes an agreement or a farewell between two parties. When you shake hands with someone leaving, it marks the end of a relationship.

Put them together — golden handshake — and you get a rich, generous farewell deal between a company and a departing employee.
Who Gets a Golden Handshake?

Golden handshakes are not for ordinary employees. They are typically reserved for:

  • CEOs (Chief Executive Officers)
  • CFOs (Chief Financial Officers)
  • Board members and directors
  • Senior executives and top-level managers

Basically, the higher up you are in a company, the more likely you are to receive one. A regular office worker or factory employee would not typically receive a golden handshake. They might receive a standard severance package, which is far more modest and routine.
What Does a Golden Handshake Actually Include?

A golden handshake is rarely just a single cheque. It is usually a package of financial benefits bundled together. It can include any combination of the following:

Lump-sum cash payment. This is the most straightforward part — a direct, one-time payment of money. This amount can be in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions of dollars (or any other currency), depending on the executive's seniority and the terms of their contract.

Stock or shares in the company. The executive may be given company stocks as part of the deal, which they can hold or sell. Since senior executives often already own company shares, this can be enormously valuable.

Pension benefits. The package often includes a boosted pension — meaning the executive receives more retirement money than they would have if they had simply resigned normally.

Continued health insurance or medical benefits. Even after leaving the company, the departing executive may continue to receive health coverage for a period of time.

Extended use of company perks. Things like a company car, private jet access, housing allowance, or club memberships might continue for a defined period post-departure.

Consulting fees. Sometimes companies agree to pay the departing executive as a "consultant" for a period after they leave, even if the person does little to no actual consulting work. This is often a way to spread out the payout and make it look more acceptable.

Not every golden handshake includes all of these — the exact composition depends on what was agreed upon in the executive's original employment contract.
The Key Point: It Is Often Pre-Agreed

This is crucial to understand. In most cases, a golden handshake is not a surprise bonus invented on the day someone leaves. It is typically written into the executive's contract from the very beginning, before they even start the job.

When a company hires a powerful CEO, for example, the CEO's lawyer and the company's lawyer negotiate an entire employment agreement. Buried within that agreement is often a severance clause — a section that spells out exactly what happens financially if the executive leaves or is removed. This pre-agreed payout is the golden handshake.

This matters because it means the company legally agreed to pay this amount upfront, long before the departure ever happened. It is a binding obligation, not a voluntary gift.
Why Do Companies Offer Golden Handshakes?

From the company's point of view, offering a golden handshake makes sense for several reasons.

To attract top talent. The most skilled and sought-after executives have enormous choices. Competing companies all want them. By promising a generous exit package in the event things don't work out, a company makes itself more attractive to hire. It reassures the executive: "Even if this goes wrong, you will be taken care of."

To remove someone cleanly and quickly. When a company needs to remove a CEO — perhaps because the company is underperforming, or because there is a strategic shift — it wants the process to be fast and quiet. A large financial settlement encourages the departing person to leave without creating legal battles, negative publicity, or bitter public disputes. Money smooths the exit.

To enforce silence. Golden handshake agreements almost always come with a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), which legally prevents the departing executive from speaking negatively about the company, sharing internal secrets, or criticising the board in public. The golden handshake essentially buys the executive's silence and cooperation.

To prevent the person from joining a rival. The agreement may include a non-compete clause, which prevents the departing executive from working for a competing company for a set period of time — often one to two years. The golden handshake financially compensates them for this period during which they cannot work in their industry.

To honour a legal and moral obligation. If the company is restructuring, merging, or downsizing and must lay off its executive leadership — even when those executives did nothing wrong — the golden handshake is simply the fair and agreed-upon compensation for ending the contract early.
Two Main Scenarios Where It Happens

Golden handshakes occur in two broad situations:

1. Involuntary departure (the company pushes the person out)

This is the most common scenario. The board of directors decides they want a new CEO, or the company merges with another organisation and there is no longer a need for the current executive. The person is not being fired for doing something wrong — they are simply being let go due to business circumstances. The golden handshake rewards them for their service and compensates them for the sudden loss of their job.

2. Voluntary early retirement

Sometimes a company wants to reduce its workforce during tough economic times. Instead of mass redundancies at the lower levels, they encourage senior (and often highly-paid) employees to retire early by sweetening the deal. They essentially say: "If you agree to retire now rather than in five years, we will give you a very generous payout." This benefits the company by reducing payroll costs, and benefits the employee by securing their financial future ahead of schedule.
The Controversy Around Golden Handshakes

Golden handshakes are deeply controversial, and this is where it gets interesting.

The core criticism is that executives sometimes receive enormous golden handshakes even when they have performed poorly — or even when their decisions actively harmed the company and its shareholders. Critics argue this rewards failure, which is fundamentally unfair. It sends the message: "You can run this company into the ground, and we'll still pay you millions on your way out."

Imagine a CEO who leads a company for three years, during which the company's share price falls dramatically, thousands of employees are laid off, and profits collapse. That CEO is then removed by the board — and walks away with a $20 million golden handshake. Shareholders, employees, and the general public often find this deeply unjust.

The other major criticism is the sheer scale of these packages. While an ordinary worker might receive a few weeks of redundancy pay when they lose their job, a senior executive receives what is often a life-changing sum. This disparity fuels anger about inequality within corporations.

However, defenders of golden handshakes make a valid counter-argument. They say that:

  • The amounts were agreed upon in a legal contract, and contracts must be honoured.
  • The packages are necessary to attract world-class talent.
  • Without such protection, the best executives would never take the risk of leaving a secure position to lead a large company.
  • Not all golden handshakes are for poor performers — many are simply the cost of a necessary organisational change.
A Golden Handshake vs. Standard Redundancy Pay — What's the Difference?

When any regular employee is made redundant (let go due to the role being eliminated rather than poor performance), they usually receive standard redundancy pay, which is a modest, legally mandated amount based on their years of service and salary. It follows a fixed formula set by law.

A golden handshake, on the other hand, is negotiated individually, is almost always much larger than standard redundancy pay, and is given to senior figures as part of a bespoke contractual agreement. It is not a legal requirement — it is a privately negotiated deal. The two are entirely different in scale and nature.
The Golden Family: Related Terms You Should Know

The business world has several "golden" terms, and confusing them is very common. Here is a clear distinction:

Golden Handshake — A large payout when a senior executive leaves the company (departure benefit).

Golden Parachute — Very similar to a golden handshake, but the term is specifically used when an executive loses their job due to a company takeover or acquisition. It is the financial cushion that softens the fall when one company buys another and the old leadership is replaced. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but technically a golden parachute is a subset of the golden handshake concept, specifically tied to mergers and acquisitions.

Golden Handcuffs — This is the opposite concept. Instead of a leaving payment, golden handcuffs are financial incentives designed to keep an employee at the company. These might include bonuses that only pay out after five years of service, stock options that vest gradually, or special benefits that disappear if the employee resigns. They "handcuff" the person to the company by making it financially painful to leave.

Golden Hello — This is a large signing bonus paid when an executive joins a company, to entice them away from their current employer. It is the welcome gift, whereas the golden handshake is the farewell gift.

So the full lifecycle looks like this: a company pays a golden hello to bring someone in, golden handcuffs to keep them there, and a golden handshake to let them go.
A Simple Real-World Example to Cement Your Understanding

Imagine a large technology company — let's call it TechCorp — that hires a new CEO named Sarah. When Sarah is hired, her contract states:

"If Sarah is removed from her role or if the company is sold within the first five years, she will receive a lump-sum payment of $15 million, plus two years of health insurance, plus immediate vesting of all her company shares."

Three years later, TechCorp is acquired by a larger company. Sarah's role is eliminated. She walks away with the $15 million, her health insurance, and her shares — all of which were already promised to her in her contract. That is her golden handshake.

Was it fair? That depends on who you ask. But it was legal, contractual, and agreed upon by both parties from the very beginning.
The Core Takeaway

A golden handshake is a pre-negotiated, large financial exit package given to high-ranking executives when they depart a company — voluntarily or otherwise. It exists because top executives command enormous bargaining power, companies need to attract and smoothly remove leadership, and business contracts are binding agreements that must be honoured.

It rewards the executive for their service, compensates them for losing their position, purchases their silence and cooperation, and prevents messy, public legal battles. Whether it is just or unjust is one of the great ongoing debates in corporate governance — but there is no doubt that golden handshakes remain a standard feature of executive-level employment across the world.
